impending

im-PEND-ing — the root means 'to hang'; something impending hangs over you, about to happen. · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Impending is about to happen or occur, used for something threatening or unwelcome.

Dark storm clouds gathering on the horizon signaled the impending hurricane.

Example

Factory workers notice their supervisors holding unusually long, quiet meetings behind closed doors for three days straight, and by the end of the week the same unconfirmed rumor of impending company-wide cuts has reached everyone in the building.

That sense that something serious and unwelcome is about to happen, even before it's officially announced, is what impending captures. Impending is a close cousin of imminent (both mean 'about to happen'), though impending often carries a slightly more ominous, threatening tone.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

imminent: Imminent means about to happen very soon -- it is purely about timing and says nothing about whether the coming event is good or bad. Impending shares the nearness but adds a warning tone: an impending storm or deadline feels serious or unwelcome, while an imminent arrival can be happy news.

forthcoming: Forthcoming means coming soon, with no dark overtone -- a forthcoming album or election is simply on its way. Impending also points to something coming, but it warns you: the event is usually threatening or unwelcome. Good news is forthcoming; a crisis is impending.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

distant: far off in time or space

remote: unlikely to happen soon, or far removed

Where it sits · how threatening the coming event feels

approaching → impending → looming

approaching vs. impending: Approaching is more neutral than impending -- approaching can describe anything getting closer, good or bad, while impending usually carries a sense that something serious or threatening is coming.

looming vs. impending: Looming can feel even more ominous than impending: impending simply means something is about to happen, but looming often adds a sense of dread, like a shadow growing larger.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — im- (in-): upon, over (Latin)

root — -pend-: to hang (Latin (pendere))

suffix — -ing: forming an adjective from a verb (Old English)

Put it together: Latin im- ('upon, over') plus pendere ('to hang'), with the -ing ending turning the verb into an adjective. Something impending literally hangs over the present moment, about to fall.

Use the root in a new word: pendant: One pendant in the museum's collection is more than two thousand years old.
